claims.text: Mechanical-performance differences among equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi and its FCC quaternary and ternary subsets arise from local chemical short-range order rather than constituent count alone.
Local chemical ordering is associated with changes in stacking-fault energy.
Changes in stacking-fault energy alter partial-dislocation activity and deformation-induced fault or twin formation.
The quinary alloy and the relevant equiatomic quaternary and ternary derivatives can all be prepared as single-phase FCC materials after thermomechanical processing.
Local chemical ordering influences the immobilization or spacing of partial dislocations.
Short-range-order-mediated changes in partial dislocations affect faulting, twinning, or FCC-to-HCP transformation tendencies.
Chemical fluctuations create local regions with altered stacking-fault energy.
Local stacking-fault-energy variations facilitate or impede partial-dislocation slip and the nucleation or propagation of faults and deformation twins.
Progressive faulting, twinning, or phase transformation changes strain-hardening behavior.
Relative to CrMnFeCoNi, reduced-component alloys with stronger short-range order will develop higher densities of stable stacking faults or deformation twins.
Higher densities of deformation faults, twins, or transformation products will increase strain-hardening rates.
Increased strain hardening will produce higher strength and/or ductility than in the quinary baseline.
CrMnFeCoNi is an established single-phase alloy suitable as the compositional baseline.
The proposed mechanism applies from cryogenic to ambient temperatures when the alloys remain single-phase FCC and have comparable grain size and thermomechanical history.
Magnetically driven transformations may contribute to differences among the alloys independently of short-range order.
Impurity content may contribute to the mechanical-property differences.
